rationale: B wins because it knows when to kill the shiny but underproved angle. Its refusal of "Klarna proves AI customer service actually works" is the adult move: speed is not satisfaction, while A keeps "The most-mocked category of enterprise AI might actually be working" alive on evidence that cannot carry it. A has usable raw material, but B packages the strongest story as "Klarna's AI did the work of 700 agents. It won't say how many people lost their jobs." and wastes less space pretending duplicates are new angles.
gaps_in_A: "The most-mocked category of enterprise AI might actually be working" overclaims the evidence. The update gives speed and volume, not satisfaction, accuracy, reopen rates, or actual customer outcomes.

"Klarna's AI is now handling disputes for a base of 150 million consumers" is too firm. The facts say advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes, not that this assistant handles or decides disputes across the whole base.
"Klarna's profitability narrative leans on AI-driven cost reduction" is plausible but not proven by the update. The set asks for prospectus proof, but the angle itself still smuggles in the thesis.

The first and third angles are too close: "contextualized against the headcount trend" and "what the company withholds" are both versions of the labor-displacement story. One sharper labor/accountability angle would do more work than two padded ones.
gaps_in_B: "a chatbot may be the first one to rule on it" is a strong line but under-sourced. The update does not establish that the assistant rules on disputes or is the first decision-maker.
"The reporter will write this story with or without Klarna" is posture, not evidence. Keep the urgency, lose the crystal ball.
"completed experiment rather than a pilot" goes beyond the facts. The update says first months and a year-over-year headcount drop; it does not say Klarna completed an experiment.
"AI-shrunk cost base" is directionally attractive but needs cost proof. Headcount and resolution time are not the same thing as a measured cost-base reduction.
